papers.title: Efficacy of indocyanine green (ICG) angiography in reducing postoperative complications in oesophagectomy: systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Dermanis A, Thompson D, Kamarajah S, Griffiths E
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anastomotic leakage after oesophagectomy is common, and associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Indocyanine green (ICG) fluorescence angiography has emerged as a promising intraoperative adjunct for perfusion assessment at the anastomotic site. This study aims to assess the impact of ICG use on anastomotic leakage rates and postoperative outcomes.
METHODS: A PRISMA-compliant systematic search of Medline, PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library was performed. The primary outcome was anastomotic leakage. Key secondary outcomes were conduit necrosis, mortality, and reoperation; all secondary outcomes were reported. The Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) and Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tools were used for investigating risk of bias. Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) was used to assess certainty of evidence. A random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression as well as subgroup and sensitivity analyses were performed.
RESULTS: From 902 identified studies, 23 met the inclusion criteria (including 4 RCTs; 2845 patients, of whom 1154 underwent ICG assessment). ICG use was associated with reduced anastomotic leakage rates (OR 0.44 (95% c.i. 0.29 to 0.65), P < 0.001; number needed to treat = 13) and conduit necrosis rates (OR 0.32 (95% c.i. 0.12 to 0.85), P = 0.022). Mortality (OR 1.43 (95% c.i. 0.69 to 2.97), P = 0.335), reoperation (OR 0.84 (95% c.i. 0.51 to 1.39), P = 0.500), severe anastomotic leakage, overall morbidity, readmission, operating time, and length of stay did not differ between groups. Certainty of evidence was low or very low across all outcomes (GRADE), predominantly driven by the observational study design of many of the studies.
CONCLUSION: Use of ICG appears to be associated with reduced anastomotic leak in oesophagectomy, although certainty of evidence is low. Assessment remains qualitative and operator-dependent.

papers.title: Long-term oncological outcomes of robotic versus laparoscopic total mesorectal excision for rectal cancer: COLRAR randomized clinical trial
papers.authors: Song S, Min B, Park J, Lee K, Kim N, Kim S
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Long-term oncological equivalence of robotic total mesorectal excision (R-TME) and laparoscopic total mesorectal excision (L-TME) remains unproven. The 5-year outcomes of the COLRAR RCT are reported.
METHODS: Adults with cT1-4a Nx M0 rectal adenocarcinoma within 10 cm of the anal verge were randomized 1 : 1 to L-TME or R-TME at three Korean tertiary centres between July 2011 and February 2016. Pre-specified secondary endpoints were 5-year overall, relapse-free, local recurrence-free, and distant recurrence-free survival. Analyses were on a modified intention-to-treat basis.
RESULTS: Of 295 analysed patients (144 L-TME patients and 151 R-TME patients; median follow-up of 72.6 months), 5-year overall survival (92.6% versus 92.4%; P = 0.838) and relapse-free survival (81.9% versus 83.0%; P = 0.801) were similar. Local recurrence occurred in 4.9% (L-TME) and 1.3% (R-TME); 5-year local recurrence-free and distant recurrence-free survival did not differ (P = 0.076 and P = 0.655). In a post-hoc analysis of 146 patients who received neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, 5-year local recurrence-free survival was 98.6% in R-TME patients versus 90.7% in L-TME patients (P = 0.039).
CONCLUSION: R-TME and L-TME produced equivalent 5-year oncological outcomes. A post-hoc analysis suggested improved local control with robotic surgery after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, requiring confirmation in prospectively designed studies.
REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT01423214 (http://www.clinicaltrials.gov).

papers.title: AZUR-4, a Phase 2, Open Label, Randomized Study of Neoadjuvant Dostarlimab Plus CAPEOX Versus CAPEOX in Previously Untreated T4N0 or Stage III Mismatch Repair Proficient/Microsatellite Stable Resectable Colon Cancer
papers.ptype: Clinical Trial, Phase II, Randomized Controlled Trial
papers.authors: Rasschaert G, Peddle A, Verbandt S, Tejpar S, West N, Ross J
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Recent evidence has suggested that neoadjuvant chemotherapy may provide clinical benefit for patients with locally advanced colon cancer. Immunotherapy may provide additive or synergistic effects when combined with chemotherapy. This study's objective is to assess the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of neoadjuvant dostarlimab in combination with capecitabine-oxaliplatin (CAPEOX) versus CAPEOX in patients with T4N0 or stage III mismatch repair proficient/microsatellite stable (pMMR/MSS) resectable colon cancer.
METHODS: AZUR-4 (NCT06567782) is a multicenter, phase 2, open-label, randomized (3:1 ratio) study of 120 patients across multiple countries. Eligible patients are aged ≥ 18 years with resectable pMMR/MSS colon adenocarcinoma with no prior treatment. Four cycles (21 days) of CAPEOX ± dostarlimab will be administered as neoadjuvant treatment. After completing neoadjuvant treatment, patients will undergo surgery 3 to 6 weeks later, with additional adjuvant chemotherapy administered after surgery at the investigator's discretion; no additional dostarlimab will be administered. Primary endpoints are major pathological response, determined by local assessment, and safety. Secondary endpoints will assess the feasibility and pathological response to the regimen. Exploratory endpoints include biomarker readouts and pathological response rate in biomarker subsets.
CONCLUSIONS: AZUR-4 will evaluate the effect of neoadjuvant dostarlimab + CAPEOX in patients with previously untreated T4N0 or stage III pMMR/MSS resectable colon cancer, a population for whom improved treatments are urgently needed. The robust sampling and advanced analysis of pretreatment and posttreatment blood, tissue, and tumor samples planned for this trial should assist in elucidating immune profile analyses to support the discovery of novel predictive biomarkers in this population.

papers.title: Timing of diverting ileostomy closure after low anterior resection for rectal cancer: a GRADE-assessed systematic review and meta-analysis of early and delayed closure
papers.authors: Mirza W, Ullah S, Babar M, Nand R, Hiraj U, Soomro I
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare early and delayed diverting ileostomy closure after low anterior resection for rectal cancer, focusing on postoperative morbidity and recovery outcomes, and to assess the certainty of available evidence.
METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 26th April, 2026. Five comparative studies (four randomized trials and one prospective cohort; 512 participants) were included. Random-effects meta-analyses evaluated overall post-closure morbidity as the primary outcome and severe complications, index-to-closure interval, postoperative hospital stay, operative time, and reoperation as secondary outcomes. Certainty was assessed using GRADE.
RESULTS: Overall morbidity occurred in 52/257 patients after early closure and 50/255 after delayed closure (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.66-1.71; τ²=0.12; I²=40%). Severe complications and reoperation did not differ statistically, with confidence intervals compatible with benefit or harm. The index-to-closure interval was 107.09 days shorter with early closure (95% CI - 153.01 to - 61.17; τ²=2023.39; I²=96%); this process measure was largely inherent to the group definitions. Hospital stay and operative time did not differ statistically.
CONCLUSION: The available evidence does not demonstrate a statistically significant difference in postoperative morbidity but does not establish equivalence. Early closure may be considered in selected patients after postoperative recovery and assessment of anastomotic integrity; however, these findings do not support routine early closure in all patients.

papers.title: Combined versus staged resection of synchronous rectal cancer liver metastases: national target trial emulation
papers.authors: Marchegiani F, Dhote A, Nassar A, Mallet V, Pellat A, Jeddou H
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Optimal sequencing of rectal and liver resection for patients with resectable synchronous liver metastases (SLM) from rectal cancer remains controversial, and rectal-specific evidence is limited.
METHODS: A nationwide target trial (METASYNC-R) was emulated using the French national discharge database (2014-2023). Adults undergoing both rectal and liver resection for rectal cancer with SLM were eligible. Combined resection was compared with staged strategies (rectum- or liver-first within 14 weeks). Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) estimated the average treatment effect. Thirty-day severe complications (Clavien-Dindo grade ≥III) were analysed using marginal logistic regression with robust variance; overall survival was analysed using IPTW Cox proportional hazards models with cluster-robust standard errors. Landmark analyses at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months addressed potential immortal time bias.
RESULTS: Among 9632 patients undergoing both resections, 3057 had SLM and 1872 met the eligibility criteria (median age of 64 years); 1365 (73%) underwent combined resection and 507 (27%) underwent staged resection. Severe complications occurred in 39.7% versus 45.3% (P = 0.20); combined surgery was not associated with an increased risk of severe complications (adjusted OR 0.82 (95% c.i. 0.58 to 1.16); P = 0.27). Major hepatectomy independently increased the risk of severe complications (adjusted OR 1.81 (95% c.i. 1.06 to 3.08); P = 0.029). Thirty-day mortality was similar (1.8% versus 1.5%). Median overall survival was 52.4 months (combined) versus 57.3 months (staged) (P = 0.30). Combined surgery was not associated with worse survival (adjusted HR 0.88 (95% c.i. 0.65 to 1.19); P = 0.40), with consistent findings across landmark analyses.
CONCLUSION: In this nationwide rectal cancer cohort, combined and staged strategies were associated with comparable morbidity and long-term survival. Surgical sequencing should be individualized within multidisciplinary decision-making.
Combined or staged surgery for rectal cancer with liver spread: which approach is safer? Background and aim Nearly one-third of patients with rectal cancer present with liver metastases at diagnosis. When both sites can be removed, surgeons can operate in one session (combined surgery) or in two steps (staged surgery). The authors compared both strategies for safety and survival. Method The authors used data from all French hospitals (2014–2023) and found 1872 patients who had both rectal and liver surgery. The authors used a method that mimics a clinical trial, using hospital records to make the comparison as fair as possible. Findings Serious problems after surgery—needing further surgery or intensive care—occurred in about 40% of patients in both groups. Median survival was 52 months after combined surgery and 57 months after staged surgery. Neither result was clearly better. Conclusion Neither approach was clearly safer or led to better survival. The choice should be made case by case in a specialist team, based on each patient’s own case.

papers.title: A comparison of extended right hemicolectomy and transverse colectomy with D3 lymph node dissection for pathological stage II/III advanced mid-transverse colon cancer
papers.authors: Ota E, Ozawa M, Nakagawa K, Suwa H, Suwa Y, Endo I
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: To date, no study has focused exclusively on D3 lymph node dissection for mid-transverse colon cancer. The present study compared surgical and oncological results following extended right hemicolectomy (exRHC) and transverse colectomy (TC) with standardized D3 lymphadenectomy in patients with locally advanced mid-transverse colon cancer.
METHODS: Patients with stage II or III mid-transverse colon cancer who underwent D3 lymphadenectomy with central ligation of the middle colic artery (MCA) between January 2013 and December 2022 were divided into two groups by surgical procedure. We compared patient short- and long-term outcomes between the groups.
RESULTS: Eighty-three patients (exRHC, n = 56; TC, n = 27) were analyzed. Overall complication rates (35.7% vs. 22.2%, p = 0.458) and Clavien-Dindo grade ≥ 3 complications (10.7% vs. 3.7%, p = 0.418) did not differ significantly between the exRHC and TC groups. In contrast, postoperative ileus occurred more frequently in the exRHC group (16.1% vs. 0%, p = 0.028), and the hospitalization duration was significantly longer in the exRHC group (8 vs. 7 days, p = 0.016). The 3-year relapse free survival (RFS) was 86.3% for exRHC and 80.3% for TC (p = 0.63), and the 3-year overall survival (OS) was 92.6% and 91.6%, respectively (p = 0.778).
CONCLUSIONS: In advanced mid-transverse colon cancer with D3 lymph node dissection and central MCA ligation, exRHC associated with a higher risk of postoperative ileus and longer hospital stay than TC. Given similar oncologic outcomes, TC may be a more favorable surgical option owing to its faster recovery.

papers.title: Online Information-Seeking Behaviour for Major Cancers: A 10-Year Infodemiological Study to Inform Public Health and Health Promotion Priorities in Hungary
papers.authors: Gajdács M, Ilić I, Szabó-Kurucz D, Molnár R, Paulik E, Elmer D
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: To analyse trends in online information-seeking behaviour for five major cancers in Hungary, compare them with global trends, and assess changes during the COVID-19 pandemic, cancer-related awareness campaigns, and major cancer-related events on search activity. Methods: A retrospective observational infodemiological study was conducted using Google Trends™ (GT) data for lung, colorectal, breast, prostate, and pancreatic cancers between 2013 and 2022. Search intensity was assessed using uncorrected relative search volume (RSVraw) as the primary measure, complemented by RSVsens, as an Internet penetration-adjusted sensitivity analysis. Descriptive statistics, parametric tests, time-series and seasonality analyses, Mann-Kendall tests, and joinpoint regression were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics 22.0, PAST 4.03, and Joinpoint 5.3.0 (α: 0.05; 95% confidence interval [CI]). Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied for multiple testing. Results: Among the cancer types relevant to our study, lung and breast cancer showed the highest reference-adjusted RSV (RSVref: 61) in Hungary, followed by prostate (RSVref: 59), colorectal (RSVref: 52), and pancreatic cancer (RSVref: 11); whereas globally, breast cancer ranked first (RSVref: 49). RSVsens showed significant decreasing trends for all five cancer types (Mann-Kendall, all p < 0.05), with average annual percentage changes (AAPCs) of -5.39% for lung, -4.06% for breast, -3.56% for colorectal, -3.59% for prostate, and -5.23% for pancreatic cancer, respectively (all p < 0.05). Breast and prostate cancers exhibited significant (p < 0.001) and recurring seasonal peaks. During COVID-19 (vs. the pre-pandemic period), mean RSV values decreased by 10-30% across all cancers; only colorectal cancer-related campaigns were associated with a notable increase in search intensity (+66.9%, p = 0.013, q = 0.058), although this association did not remain significant after FDR correction.. Symptom-related searches predominated, whereas screening- and prevention-related queries were infrequent during the study period. Conclusions: GT may be a useful complementary tool for monitoring public interest and evaluating public health communication. The absence of consistent increases in search activity during most campaign periods, together with the predominance of symptom-related queries, suggests that current communication initiatives may have limited measurable visibility in GT search behaviour and highlights the need to strengthen communication on cancer prevention and early detection.

papers.title: The Traditional Chinese Medicine-Gut Microbiota-Colorectal Cancer Axis: Mechanistic Insights and Recent Progress
papers.journal_full: The American journal of Chinese medicine
papers.authors: Wang B, Dong Y, Liu K, Li S, Huang Y, Li A
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of global cancer mortality, with gut microbiota (GM) dysbiosis playing a critical role in its pathogenesis. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) offers a holistic, multi-target approach and has shown increasing promise in CRC prevention and treatment through GM modulation. This review systematically proposes the "TCM-GM-CRC" axis and elucidates seven interconnected mechanisms through which it mediates the anti-CRC effects of TCM: Reshaping microbial balance by inhibiting pathogens and enriching probiotics; repairing intestinal barrier integrity through upregulation of tight junction proteins and mucin production; suppressing oncogenic and pro-inflammatory signaling pathways by pathogenic bacteria; remodeling the tumor immune microenvironment through immunocyte regulation; modulating microbial metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and tryptophan derivatives; intervening in CRC cell metabolic reprogramming, including aerobic glycolysis and aberrant lipid metabolism; and inhibiting epithelial-mesenchymal transition and metastasis. Key herbal formulas and active compounds discussed include Canmei Formula, Wu Mei Wan, Gegen Qinlian Decoction, Banxia Xiexin Decoction, and Pien Tze Huang, as well as single compounds such as berberine, evodiamine, curcumin, ginsenoside Rh4, and sophocarpine, which exert anti-CRC effects through distinct GM-mediated pathways. We emphasize the synergistic and multi-dimensional role of TCM in targeting GM and its functional metabolites to combat CRC. To deepen the understanding of the "TCM-GM-CRC" interaction mechanisms, future research should integrate multi-omics technologies, germ-free models, fecal microbiota transplantation, and clinical translation. Additionally, the development of "TCM-plus" combinatorial strategies, microbiota-targeted nanodelivery systems, and medically formulated foods is advocated to advance CRC precision prevention and treatment centered on GM.

papers.title: Colorectal cancers with distinct metastatic potential trigger divergent early T cell responses
papers.authors: Saad M, Thoms A, Yin Y, Mamede I, Rahman A, Chen R
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of mortality, with most cases refractory to immunotherapy. Distinguishing tumor-induced from steady-state mucosal T cell responses represents a critical barrier to understanding CRC immunity. Using orthotopic transplantation of CRC organoids with and without metastatic potential, combined with T cell fate-mapping, we show that nonmetastatic tumors elicit early recruitment of CD8αβ+ and CD4+ T cells with cytotoxic and Th1-like programs, whereas pro-metastatic (pro-Met) tumors induce a naïve-like, hypoactivated state. Tumor-infiltrating CD4+ T cells underwent clonal expansion, including clones recognizing microbial and dietary antigens. T cells physically interacting with tumors, identified by universal LIPSTIC, were enriched for expanded and cytotoxic clones. Fate-mapped T cells from nonmetastatic tumors suppressed tumor growth in an IFN-γ-dependent manner. Mechanistically, pro-Met tumors downregulated MHCII, and Ciita targeting in nonmetastatic organoids reduced CD4+ clonal expansion and led to tumor progression. Together, these findings define divergent early T cell trajectories associated with CRC metastasis, indicating that ineffective local immune engagement precedes metastatic dissemination.

papers.title: From Dysbiosis to Symbiosis: Using the Gut Microbiome to Improve Cancer Outcomes
papers.abstract: The gut microbiome has emerged as an important regulator of cancer biology, influencing carcinogenesis, treatment response, and therapy-related toxicity. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the mechanistic roles of the gut microbiota in gastrointestinal (GI) cancers and evaluates emerging microbiome-based strategies for improving cancer outcomes. Dysbiosis-characterized by altered microbial diversity, depletion of beneficial functions, and enrichment of disease-associated taxa-may contribute to tumorigenesis through interconnected mechanisms involving chronic inflammation, genotoxicity, metabolic dysregulation, epigenetic alterations, and immune evasion. Key cancer-associated bacteria, including Fusobacterium nucleatum, enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis (ETBF), pks+Escherichia coli, and Helicobacter pylori, illustrate the mechanistic diversity of microbiota-associated carcinogenesis. Beyond cancer initiation, the gut microbiome can influence the efficacy and toxicity of anticancer therapies. In immunotherapy, specific microbial taxa and metabolites modulate antitumor immunity and immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) responses, while antibiotic-associated dysbiosis has been linked to poorer outcomes. In chemotherapy, microbial metabolism and microbiota-derived metabolites can alter drug efficacy and toxicity, including modulation of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) activity. Microbiome-based biomarkers show promise for cancer detection and treatment prediction, with fecal microbial signatures, including F. nucleatum, potentially improving colorectal cancer (CRC) screening when incorporated into multimarker strategies. Therapeutic approaches aimed at restoring microbial symbiosis include fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), which has shown preliminary potential to restore ICI responsiveness in treatment-refractory melanoma, and probiotic interventions, although clinical evidence remains limited. Emerging engineered microbial therapeutics, including tumor-targeting bacteria designed to deliver localized immunostimulatory payloads, are advancing toward clinical translation. Despite substantial progress, important challenges remain, including methodological heterogeneity, lack of standardized protocols, confounding factors, and unresolved safety concerns. Personalized strategies integrating microbial features with host characteristics and treatment context may ultimately enable more effective microbiome-based approaches to improve cancer outcomes.

papers.title: Marine-Derived Polysaccharides Against Ulcerative Colitis: Sources, Structures, and Multi-Target Mechanisms
papers.authors: Zheng D, Wang X, Xiang Y, Wei S, Chen R, Lu Q
papers.abstract: Marine-derived polysaccharides have emerged as promising bioactive candidates for alleviating ulcerative colitis (UC), a chronic inflammatory bowel disease with limited therapeutic options. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in the sources, preparation methods, structural features, and multi-target mechanisms of these polysaccharides from seaweeds, marine animals, and microorganisms. Key physicochemical parameters, including molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, glycosidic linkages, and sulfation patterns, critically influence their anti-colitis efficacy. Mechanistically, these macromolecules synergistically restore gut microbiota homeostasis (e.g., promoting short-chain fatty acids and secondary bile acids), suppress inflammatory pathways (NF-κB, MAPK, and NLRP3), regulate immune responses (inhibiting dendritic cell and Th1/Th17 activation), alleviate oxidative stress via the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway, and reinforce intestinal epithelial barrier integrity (upregulating tight junction proteins and mucins). Although systematic toxicological characterization remains limited, the generally favorable safety profiles reported in preclinical studies, together with their multi-target nature, suggest that marine polysaccharides hold great potential as functional foods or adjunctive therapies for UC. However, challenges remain in structural heterogeneity, batch-to-batch consistency, and limited clinical validation. Future efforts should prioritize structure-activity relationship elucidation, advanced analytical characterization, bioavailability and gastrointestinal fate studies, standardization and quality control, comparative evaluation against conventional therapies and other natural products, and well-designed clinical trials to facilitate translation from bench to bedside.

papers.title: Robotic rectal cancer surgery: oncological and functional outcomes, technical pitfalls, and unresolved controversies
papers.authors: Zhu X, Yang X, Wang T, Wang T, Wang Y, Wang Y
papers.abstract: Total mesorectal excision (TME) remains the curative operation for rectal cancer. The male pelvis, obesity, and a narrow anal canal make rectal dissection the most demanding step in abdominal surgery, even for experienced surgeons. Robotic systems were introduced to address these constraints by providing a stable three-dimensional view, wristed instruments, and ergonomic control beyond that of conventional laparoscopy. Two decades after the first robotic TME, randomized trials (ROLARR and REAL), transanal TME trials, and more than a dozen meta-analyses permit a more measured assessment. To make that assessment clear and comparable, we organize it around a prespecified core set of outcome parameters rather than every metric reported in the literature: the primary oncological and surgical-quality outcomes are conversion to open surgery, circumferential resection margin (CRM) involvement, completeness of the mesorectal specimen, and long-term locoregional recurrence and disease-free survival; the primary functional outcomes are bowel, urinary, and sexual function, measured with validated instruments at fixed time points. Overall survival, distal margin, lymph node yield, general morbidity and anastomotic leak, operative time, blood loss, length of stay, quality of life, and cost are treated as secondary outcomes. Against this core set, robotic surgery consistently reduces conversion to open surgery. In the most informative recent trial, it also improved circumferential resection margin quality and three-year locoregional control in high-risk middle and low rectal cancers, without affecting overall survival. Functional benefits, including earlier recovery of urinary function and modest improvements in bowel and sexual outcomes, are plausible but supported by low-certainty evidence. Distinct pitfalls remain, ranging from arm collision and docking errors to distal-plane deviation and anastomotic failure, and the approach is slower and more expensive than laparoscopy. This review summarizes the oncological and functional evidence, relates technical errors to the operative sequence, and examines unresolved controversies: which patients benefit most, how robotics compares with transanal dissection, and whether fluorescence imaging, neuromonitoring, and new competing platforms alter the balance.

papers.title: Circulating Tumor DNA (ctDNA) for Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) Detection in Colorectal Cancer (CRC): Current Evidence, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions
papers.authors: Hyde H, Mageau E, Leduc C, Madhu M, Dickinson N, Nisa T
papers.abstract: Minimal residual disease (MRD) is a major contributor to colorectal cancer (CRC) recurrence following curative-intent treatment, yet conventional surveillance methods may fail to detect residual disease at its earliest stages. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has emerged as a minimally invasive biomarker for MRD detection and postoperative monitoring. We conducted a structured PubMed-based literature review and included 94 publications evaluating ctDNA in CRC. Across the literature, postoperative ctDNA positivity was consistently associated with increased recurrence risk and poorer disease-free and overall survival, while serial monitoring improved detection sensitivity and enabled assessment of treatment response. ctDNA frequently identified molecular recurrence approximately 2.5-11.5 months before conventional surveillance. Both tumor-informed and tumor-naive strategies were represented, using PCR/ddPCR, targeted next-generation sequencing, whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, methylation-based assays, and emerging multiomic approaches. Although ctDNA demonstrates strong prognostic value, evidence supporting treatment modification based solely on ctDNA status remains limited. Further prospective randomized trials, assay standardization, and consensus clinical guidelines are required before routine implementation. Overall, ctDNA is a promising tool for recurrence prediction, surveillance, and precision management of CRC.
